solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Work includes book rest trashed? Author's to make a racket

indicators.note: one word that includes others holds them inside itself, so the letters go into the middle of the work

parts.note: to operate is to work, as a machine does

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked and thrown about, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A writer's working space, stacked with books, is wrecked and they want to make a racket about it.
explanation.walkthrough: OBSTREPERATE goes O(B+STRE)PERATE. 'Author's' tells you the word belongs to one writer: Chambers credits it to Laurence Sterne.
explanation.definitionFit: Obstreperous means noisy and unruly, and this rare verb from the same root means to behave that way, raising a din.

clue.text: Chemical compound processed in lab tray left out

indicators.note: material that is processed is worked over and changed, so the letters are put in a new order
the abbreviation for left is to be left out, so that letter is dropped from the words

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: A chemical is being prepared in a laboratory tray that someone has left out on the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the L from LABTRAY, then jumble the six letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Baryta is barium oxide (or hydroxide), a compound of the metal barium used in industry and laboratories.

clue.text: Preacher and prophet, jolly individual at heart

indicators.note: what lies at the heart of something sits in its centre, so the other pieces go into the middle of the prophet

parts.note: a seer foresees the future, like a prophet
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
one individual is one

explanation.surface: A cheerful man of the cloth is described as preacher, prophet and jolly fellow all in one.
explanation.walkthrough: SE(RM+ONE)ER. 'Jolly' looks like a describing word but is the crossword's old slang for a marine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sermoneer is an old word for someone who delivers sermons, that is, a preacher.

clue.text: Heads for repast in hall after taking in college buttery?

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it within, so the college abbreviation goes inside the other letters
heads are the tops of things, so only the opening letter of each following word is kept

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: Students heading to dinner in the college hall pass the buttery, the pantry where food and drink are kept.
explanation.walkthrough: RI(C)H. A college buttery is a storeroom for provisions, but the question mark invites reading 'buttery' as full of butter.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is buttery is heavy with fat and cream, which is what we call rich food.

clue.text: Small estate left remaining as legal right

indicators.note: making the word small means cutting it short, so its ending is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened
what is left or remaining is over, as in 'food left over'

explanation.surface: A modest estate is what remains, and the heir holds it as a legal right.
explanation.walkthrough: ESTATE loses its last three letters to give EST.
explanation.definitionFit: An estover is a tenant's old legal entitlement to take wood or other necessities from the land they occupy.

clue.text: Crown circles head of tsar expanding towards the end

indicators.note: to circle something is to surround it, so the crown goes all the way round the selected letter

parts.note: the crown of the head is the pate

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening, so only its first letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of tsar

explanation.surface: A crown sits around the head of a tsar, its shape widening towards the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: PAT(T)E. 'Crown' suggests royal regalia, fitting the tsar, but it means the top of a head.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a cross patté has arms that are narrow at the centre and widen out at their tips.

clue.text: They convey one to faraway place, rugged shoreline, hard going

definitions.text: They convey one to faraway place

indicators.note: a rugged coast is broken and irregular, so these letters are broken up and rearranged
the abbreviation for hard is going away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Travellers are carried off to a remote spot where the rugged shoreline makes the going tough.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the H out of SHORELINE and rearrange what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: To eloin is an old legal verb meaning to remove or carry off to a distance, so eloiners are those who take someone far away.

clue.text: On being dismissed by judge, past caring?

definitions.note: an archaic verb, to care; 'past' flags its age

indicators.note: something dismissed is sent away, so the little word is struck out of the judge

parts.note: to reckon is to judge or estimate
taken as written; this is what is removed

explanation.surface: A case thrown out by the judge leaves someone beyond caring.
explanation.walkthrough: RECKON minus ON. 'Past caring' reads as an idiom for indifference, but here 'past' marks the word as a bygone one for caring.
explanation.definitionFit: Reck is an old verb meaning to heed or care, surviving in reckless; it belongs to past usage, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Continues without changing in dull woolly stuff

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it, so the short word goes within the word for dull

parts.note: tame means dull, unexciting
something that stays as is continues unchanged; is means exists, goes on

explanation.surface: Someone keeps wearing the same drab woollen clothes without ever changing them.
explanation.walkthrough: TAM(IS)E. 'Without changing' points to the phrase 'as is', meaning left unaltered.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamise is a thin worsted fabric, a woollen material also called tammy.

clue.text: Fruit from Bengal cored and mashed

indicators.note: mashed fruit is squashed into a new form, so the remaining letters are rearranged
a cored apple has its middle cut out, so the central letters of the word are removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fruit from Bengal is prepared by removing its core and mashing the flesh.
explanation.walkthrough: BENGAL loses its middle NG, leaving BEAL to rearrange. Fittingly, the fruit grows in India.
explanation.definitionFit: The bael is the Bengal quince, an Indian tree whose hard-shelled fruit is eaten and used in medicine.

clue.text: Group with lead vocalist securing right collar fastener

parts.note: a band is a musical group

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, here by wrapping round the abbreviation for right

parts.note: Sting was lead singer of the Police
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A pop group and its lead singer fasten the singer's collar correctly before going on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: BAND + ST(R)ING. The lead vocalist is a specific one: Sting of the band the Police.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandstring is a tie or cord used to fasten a band, the old-fashioned collar or neckband.

clue.text: Porter turned sour almost entirely, say, with a traveller's tip

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the word for entirely is dropped

parts.note: all means entirely, as in 'all alone'; cut short
e.g. means for example, as 'say' does
taken as written

indicators.note: a tip is an end point, so only the final letter of traveller is kept

parts.note: the last letter of traveller

explanation.surface: A railway porter grows almost entirely sour, despite the tip a traveller hands him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porter' looks like a railway worker but is the dark beer, and 'tip' looks like a gratuity but means the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Alegar is vinegar made from ale, literally sour ale, so a beer such as porter that has gone off.

clue.text: Tough grass nurses simmering hatred, ready to baste again?

indicators.note: to nurse something is to hold it close, so the grass wraps around the jumbled letters

parts.note: reed is a tall, tough grass

indicators.note: something simmering bubbles and churns, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A cook nursing a simmering grudge stands ready to baste the roast once more.
explanation.walkthrough: RE(THREAD)ED. 'Baste' suggests cooking, but it also means tacking cloth with long stitches, which needs a threaded needle.
explanation.definitionFit: To baste in sewing is to tack with loose stitches; a needle given thread a second time is ready to do it again.

clue.text: Alert to hear decision college is involved in

indicators.note: something involved in another is caught up inside it, so the college abbreviation sits within the decision

parts.note: an arret is a judgment or decision of a court, from French arrêt
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A college is caught up in a ruling and waits keenly to hear the decision.
explanation.walkthrough: ARRE(C)T. 'To hear' seems to belong with 'decision', but it completes the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrect describes ears pricked up, so it means attentive and on the alert for sound.

clue.text: Future punishment imposed on the writer (6, two words)

parts.note: toco is old slang for punishment, a thrashing
the writer refers to the setter, me

explanation.surface: Someone foresees punishment being imposed on them in the future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imposed on' puts one piece on top of the other, which in an across clue means before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Things to come are future ones, as in 'the world to come', so the phrase works as an adjective for later.

clue.text: One with constituency in city house — she has irresistible urges

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it, so the politician goes within the city abbreviation

parts.note: NY is the abbreviation for New York
a Member of Parliament represents a constituency
HO is the abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: An MP with a house in New York turns out to be a woman of uncontrollable desires.
explanation.walkthrough: NY(MP)HO. An MP is a member of the UK Parliament, elected by a constituency.
explanation.definitionFit: Nympho, short for nymphomaniac, is slang for a woman with compulsive sexual desire.

clue.text: Militant lot, hard one, e.g. in Germany, raised welcoming cry

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard
I is the Roman numeral for one
z.B., zum Beispiel, is German for e.g.

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising a word lifts its end to the top, so it reads upwards

parts.note: hallo is a cry of greeting

explanation.surface: A hard-line militant group in Germany raises a cheer of welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welcoming' looks like a container signal but just describes the cry, a greeting. z.B. is the standard German abbreviation for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hizbollah is a militant Shia Islamist organisation based in Lebanon, a group or body of fighters.

clue.text: Baccy cakes, new, in hollow bowl?

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it, so the abbreviation for new goes within the words for hollow and bowl

parts.note: a cave is a hollow in rock
N is the abbreviation for new
a dish is a bowl

explanation.surface: Fresh tobacco cakes are put in the hollow of a pipe bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVE + N + DISH. 'Bowl' fits the pipe-smoking scene, but here it is just a dish. Baccy is informal for tobacco.
explanation.definitionFit: Cavendish is tobacco softened, sweetened and pressed into cakes or plugs.

clue.text: Physicist using volume to wedge faulty Aga door

indicators.note: a wedge is driven into a gap, so the volume abbreviation is pushed inside the jumbled letters
something faulty is not in working order, so these letters are put out of their order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled
V is the abbreviation for volume

explanation.surface: A physicist wedges a book under the broken door of his Aga stove.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a heavy cast-iron range cooker found in British country kitchens. Volume also fits the physicist: Avogadro's law concerns gas volumes.
explanation.definitionFit: Amedeo Avogadro was an Italian scientist who proposed that equal volumes of gases hold equal numbers of molecules.

clue.text: Blood in arms necessitates angioplasty? Only some of it

indicators.note: only some of it means just a portion of the preceding words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the boundary between these two words

explanation.surface: Blood in the arms makes a heart operation necessary, though perhaps only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms' means heraldry, not limbs. Angioplasty is a procedure for widening blocked arteries.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry, sang is the term for blood, borrowed from the French word.

clue.text: When it's not run out, love getting into popular tipple, excellent Scotch

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it, so the shortened love goes within the drink

parts.note: beer is a popular drink

indicators.note: it here refers to love, which must be without the cricket abbreviation for run out

parts.note: love is zero in tennis
RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out; this is removed

explanation.surface: A popular drink keeps flowing as long as it hasn't run out, which is excellent, says a Scot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' refers back to love, which loses the cricket abbreviation. 'Scotch' looks like whisky, fitting the tipple, but it labels the word as Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Beezer is Scots and northern slang for something first-rate, an adjective for excellent.

clue.text: Turning tables with rook — it may get you out of a trap

definitions.text: it may get you out of a trap

indicators.note: turning the tables reverses a situation, and here the letters are turned around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
R is the chess abbreviation for rook

explanation.surface: A chess player turns the tables with a rook move, escaping a trap.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is a golf bunker, called a sand trap in the US, not a chess snare.
explanation.definitionFit: A blaster is a golf club, a sand wedge, used to blast the ball out of a bunker.

clue.text: Former rock group entering rise, a thrill

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so the band sits within the word for rise

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, a rise in the land
R.E.M. was a US rock band, disbanded in 2011

explanation.surface: A disbanded rock band rising again on stage gives fans a thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: T(REM)OR. A tor, a word common on Dartmoor, is a craggy hilltop.
explanation.definitionFit: A tremor can be a quiver of excitement or emotion, which is what a thrill is.

clue.text: Patch on last sore to be treated, limb not good

indicators.note: something to be treated is to be worked on and altered, so these letters are reshaped
not good means without the abbreviation for good, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
a leg is a limb
G is the abbreviation for good; this is removed

explanation.surface: A dressing is put on a sore that needs treating, as the injured leg is in bad shape.
explanation.walkthrough: LEG loses its G; SORE + LE is then rearranged. A last is the cobbler's foot-shaped block, not a final thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Resoling a shoe means fitting a new sole, a repair done with the shoe on the cobbler's last.

clue.text: Junior churchman, Scots one flanking bishops

indicators.note: to flank is to stand on both sides, so the Scots word goes either side of the bishops

parts.note: ae is Scots for one
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A junior cleric from Scotland stands between two bishops.
explanation.walkthrough: A(BB)E.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbé is a French title for an abbot or, more often, any lower-ranking cleric.

clue.text: French beak, beak I'll follow having afternoon in

indicators.note: a thing having another in it holds it inside, so the abbreviation for afternoon sits within the beak

parts.note: a bird's beak is its bill, and 'I'll follow' puts the letter I after it
A is short for afternoon, as in a.m./p.m. style timetable shorthand

explanation.surface: A French magistrate says he will follow on, having spent the afternoon in court.
explanation.walkthrough: B(A)ILL + I. Beak is British slang for a magistrate; the second beak is a bird's.
explanation.definitionFit: A bailli was a French royal officer who acted as magistrate in a district.

clue.text: Fancy dress gear, material for Hawaiian skirt? Probably not

definitions.text: material for Hawaiian skirt? Probably not

indicators.note: fancy describes something elaborate and made up, so these letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: Fancy dress outfits include a Hawaiian grass skirt, though maybe not one of real grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy dress' reads as a costume party, but 'Fancy' is the signal. The definition hedges because hula skirts are traditionally made of leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Reed grass is a tall grass of wetlands, plausibly a skirt material but not the usual one, hence 'Probably not'.

clue.text: Turn, most indecent, topless?

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, so a topless word loses its opening letter

parts.note: free can mean licentious or improper, so the most indecent is the freest

explanation.surface: The rudest turn on stage is one performed topless.
explanation.walkthrough: FREEST loses its F. 'Topless' fits the indecent scene, but it only removes a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Reest is a dialect verb for bacon or meat going rancid, and to turn is to go sour or bad.

clue.text: Cheap fur matched with outward appearance

parts.note: v. for versus, as when one team is matched with another
someone's air is their manner or outward look

explanation.surface: A cheap fur coat is worn with an air of grandeur to look expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: Vair was squirrel fur, a humbler lining than ermine in medieval robes.
explanation.definitionFit: Vair is the grey and white fur of a squirrel, used in medieval dress and as a heraldic tincture.

clue.text: It's old fashioned, wooden

indicators.note: something fashioned is shaped or made, so these letters are formed into a new word

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned piece of furniture is made of wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old fashioned' reads as one phrase, but 'old' is fodder and 'fashioned' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Stolid means impassive and unemotional, the same as wooden when describing a manner or performance.

clue.text: Exotic food plant: look in for a taste, turning up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning a word up makes it read from the bottom to the top
to look in on words is to search inside them, where a run of letters lies across the word breaks

parts.note: the letters run across these three words

explanation.surface: An exotic edible plant: drop by and sample some as it comes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look in for a taste' reads as an invitation to call and try some, but it asks you to search inside the words. 'Turning up' sounds like arriving.
explanation.definitionFit: Taro is a tropical plant grown for its starchy edible root, a staple in the Pacific and Asia.

clue.text: Fatal submersion from short period in much longer one, going back

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters read right to left
one thing in another is placed inside it, so the short period goes within the longer one

parts.note: an eon is an immensely long period
a day is a short period

explanation.surface: A drowning happens in a moment, set within a much longer stretch of history being looked back on.
explanation.walkthrough: E(DAY)ON, then the whole is read backwards. Noyades were mass drownings in the French Revolution at Nantes.
explanation.definitionFit: A noyade is an execution by drowning, as carried out at Nantes in 1793–94.

clue.text: Royal tax, obligation by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the word is judged on how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a tie is a binding obligation; the French word is said like it

explanation.surface: A tax owed to the king is an obligation, so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: TAILLE is said the French way, 'tie', and a tie is a duty that binds you.
explanation.definitionFit: The taille was a direct land tax levied by the French kings on commoners before the Revolution.

clue.text: Varnishes a girl variously applied to end of nails

indicators.note: variously means in several different ways, so the letters are laid out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is taken

parts.note: the final letter of nails

explanation.surface: A girl paints varnish on her nails in different ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Varnishes' fits the nail-painting scene, but the answer is a bookbinder's glaze.
explanation.definitionFit: Glair is egg-white glaze used as a size in bookbinding and gilding; to glair is to coat with it, much as one varnishes.

clue.text: Song that's recalled dead, strong Scots

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word for song is taken backwards

parts.note: a lay is a song or ballad
D is the abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: A song remembered from the dead is a powerful Scottish one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scots' labels the word as Scottish, not people from Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Yald, also yauld, is a Scots adjective meaning vigorous, active and robust.

clue.text: Runner with hip too stressed? Protein required

indicators.note: something stressed is under strain and pulled out of shape, so these letters are distorted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written except the joining word with, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A runner whose hip is also under strain needs protein to recover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' only joins the fodder words; the letters of runner, hip and too are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A neurotrophin is one of a family of proteins that promote the growth and survival of nerve cells.
